claim: Cells dedicate up to half of all protein and RNA synthesis to the production of ribosomal protein (r-protein) and RNA (rRNA) components required to assemble thousands of new ribosomes every minute.
source: Cells dedicate up to half of all protein and RNA synthesis to the production of ribosomal protein (r-protein) and RNA (rRNA) components required to assemble thousands of new ribosomes every minute (Warner, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warner, 1999, which provides published evidence for this statement.

claim: rRNAs and r-proteins are coordinately synthesized and matured in the nucleolus and cytosol, respectively, in response to growth cues.
source: rRNAs and r-proteins are coordinately synthesized and matured in the nucleolus and cytosol, respectively, in response to growth cues (Lempiäinen and Shore, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lempiäinen and Shore, 2009.

claim: R-proteins are co- and post-translationally folded, requiring general chaperones as well as dedicated chaperones called escortins.
source: R-proteins are co- and post-translationally folded, requiring general chaperones as well as dedicated chaperones called escortins (Pillet et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pillet et al., 2017.

claim: Environmental stressors, such as heat shock and viral infection, and xenobiotics, such as DNA-damaging agents used as chemotherapeutics, interfere with rRNA processing and nucleolar morphology.
source: Environmental stressors, such as heat shock and viral infection, and xenobiotics, such as DNA-damaging agents used as chemotherapeutics, interfere with rRNA processing and nucleolar morphology (Burger et al., 2010; Kos-Braun et al., 2017; Liu et al., 1996; Pelham, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Burger et al., 2010; Kos-Braun et al., 2017; Liu et al., 1996; Pelham, 1984.

claim: In zebrafish, and possibly in humans, hemizygous loss of r-protein genes can drive cancer formation.
source: In zebrafish, and possibly in humans, hemizygous loss of r-protein genes can drive cancer formation (Amsterdam et al., 2004; Goudarzi and Lindström, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amsterdam et al., 2004 and Goudarzi and Lindström, 2016.

claim: Diverse loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding r-proteins, r-protein assembly factors, and rRNA synthesis machinery result in tissue-specific pathologies in humans (ribosomopathies), such as red blood cell differentiation defects in patients with Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA).
source: Diverse loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding r-proteins, r-protein assembly factors, and rRNA synthesis machinery result in tissue-specific pathologies in humans (ribosomopathies), such as red blood cell differentiation defects in patients with Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA) (Draptchinskaia et al., 1999; Khajuria et al., 2018; Narla and Ebert, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Draptchinskaia et al., 1999; Khajuria et al., 2018; Narla and Ebert, 2010.

claim: In budding yeast, loss of r-protein genes increases stress resistance and replicative lifespan and reduces cell size and growth.
source: in budding yeast, loss of r-protein genes increases stress resistance and replicative lifespan and reduces cell size and growth (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Steffen et al., 2008, Steffen et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jorgensen et al., 2004; Steffen et al., 2008, Steffen et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in r-protein genes in C. elegans extend lifespan.
source: mutations in r-protein genes in C. elegans also extend lifespan.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text but lacks a specific citation in the extracted sentence, though it is presented as established knowledge.

claim: When ribosomes are less abundant, biomass accumulation slows and growth rates decrease.
source: As expected, when ribosomes are less abundant, biomass accumulation slows and growth rates decreases.
evidence: The claim is presented as an expected consequence based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Reduced ribosome concentrations alter global translation efficiencies, impacting the proteome in cell state–specific ways.
source: Furthermore, reduced ribosome concentrations alter global translation efficiencies, impacting the proteome in cell state–specific ways (Khajuria et al., 2018; Mills and Green, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khajuria et al., 2018 and Mills and Green, 2017.

claim: In many cases, cellular growth is affected before ribosome pools have appreciably diminished, indicating that perturbations of ribosome assembly have translation-independent or extraribosomal effects.
source: In many cases, however, cellular growth is affected before ribosome pools have appreciably diminished, indicating that perturbations of ribosome assembly have translation-independent or extraribosomal effects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from observed phenomena where growth is affected before ribosome depletion.

claim: In many ribosomopathies, excess r-proteins directly interact with and activate p53, presumably as a consequence of imbalanced r-protein stoichiometry.
source: In many ribosomopathies, excess r-proteins directly interact with and activate p53, presumably as a consequence of imbalanced r-protein stoichiometry.
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge about ribosomopathies, though the specific mechanism is described as presumed.

claim: p53 activation is not sufficient to explain the extraribosomal phenotypes observed in ribosomopathies or in model organisms experiencing disrupted ribosome biogenesis.
source: However, p53 activation is not sufficient to explain the extraribosomal phenotypes observed in ribosomopathies or in model organisms experiencing disrupted ribosome biogenesis (James et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to James et al., 2014.

claim: R-proteins produced in excess of one-another are normally surveyed by a ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation.
source: Interestingly, r-proteins produced in excess of one-another are normally surveyed by a ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation (McShane et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McShane et al., 2016.

claim: Ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation of excess r-proteins appears to prevent their aberrant aggregation.
source: which appears to prevent their aberrant aggregation (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a and Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: The rRNA processing factors Las1, Rat1, Rrp17, and Rrp44/Dis3 were depleted by 75–90% within 10–20 min of auxin addition.
source: The rRNA processing factors were depleted by 75–90% within 10–20 min of auxin addition, and precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) accumulated by 20 min, confirming that depletion of these factors rapidly interfered with rRNA processing (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D, which demonstrates protein depletion by Western blot.

claim: Precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) accumulated by 20 min after auxin addition, confirming that depletion of rRNA processing factors rapidly interfered with rRNA processing.
source: The rRNA processing factors were depleted by 75–90% within 10–20 min of auxin addition, and precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) accumulated by 20 min, confirming that depletion of these factors rapidly interfered with rRNA processing (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, which demonstrates pre-rRNA accumulation by Northern blot.

claim: Depletion of rRNA processing factors led to a detectable reduction in the level of free 60S subunits.
source: Depletion also led to a detectable reduction in the level of free 60S subunits, indicating that the cell was failing to assemble new 60S, but had no effect on the mature ribosome pool (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, which shows sucrose gradient profiles.

claim: Depletion of rRNA processing factors had no effect on the mature ribosome pool.
source: Depletion also led to a detectable reduction in the level of free 60S subunits, indicating that the cell was failing to assemble new 60S, but had no effect on the mature ribosome pool (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of each rRNA processing factor (Las1, Rat1, Rrp44, Rrp17) led to upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Remarkably, the induced genes are known targets of Heat-Shock Factor 1 (Hsf1), a conserved master transcription factor that controls protein folding and degradation capacity in stress, aging, and disease (Akerfelt et al., 2010) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E, which demonstrates upregulation of Hsf1 targets.

claim: Hsf1 directly controls ~50 genes encoding proteostasis factors, including protein folding chaperones, aggregate clearance factors, the transcription factor that regulates proteasome abundance, and ubiquitin.
source: Hsf1 directly controls ~50 genes encoding proteostasis factors, including protein folding chaperones (SSA1/4 (Hsp70), HSP82 (Hsp90), co-chaperones), aggregate clearance factors (BTN2, HSP42, HSP104), the transcription factor that regulates proteasome abundance (RPN4), and ubiquitin (UBI4) (Pincus et al., 2018; Solís et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pincus et al., 2018 and Solís et al., 2016.

claim: Upregulation of Hsf1-dependent genes coincided with an increase in Hsf1 occupancy at their promoters.
source: Upregulation of Hsf1-dependent genes coincided with an increase in Hsf1 occupancy at their promoters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hsf1 activation following rRNA processing factor depletion was independent of the translational stalling pathway (Rqc2).
source: and was independent of the translational stalling pathway (Rqc2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hsf1-target transcripts were maintained at high levels over an 80 min time-course of auxin treatment.
source: Hsf1-target transcripts, measured by Northern blot, were maintained at high levels over an 80 min time-course of auxin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depletion of several factors not involved in rRNA processing via AID did not activate Hsf1, including the RNA surveillance exonuclease Xrn1, mRNA decapping enzyme Dxo1, and transcription termination factor Rtt103.
source: Importantly, we ruled out the possibility that the depletion strategy itself resulted in Hsf1 activation. Depletion of several factors not involved in rRNA processing via AID did not activate Hsf1, including the RNA surveillance exonuclease Xrn1, mRNA decapping enzyme Dxo1, and transcription termination factor Rtt103 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Nuclear depletion of an rRNA processing factor using anchor-away led to Hsf1 activation.
source: Additionally, nuclear depletion of an rRNA processing factor using an orthogonal method that does not require proteasome-mediated degradation ('anchor-away') (Haruki et al., 2008) likewise led to Hsf1 activation
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using the anchor-away method, with citation to Haruki et al., 2008.

claim: Anchor-away depletion of another nuclear protein (not an rRNA processing factor) did not activate Hsf1.
source: whereas anchor-away depletion of another nuclear protein did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: Msn2/4-dependent ESR genes were not activated after depletion of rRNA processing factors.
source: Strikingly, Msn2/4-dependent ESR genes were not activated after depletion of rRNA processing factors (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment of WT cells with the oxidative agent diamide for 15 min potently activated both Hsf1- and Msn2/4-dependent genes.
source: By contrast, treatment of WT cells with the oxidative agent diamide for 15 min potently activated both Hsf1- and Msn2/4-dependent genes, as expected (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Highly specific activation of Hsf1 in the absence of ESR has only been observed in circumstances in which cellular proteostasis is acutely strained: treatment with azetidine-2-carboxylic acid (AZC) or overexpression of an aggregation-prone mutant protein.
source: Highly specific activation of Hsf1 in the absence of ESR has only been observed in circumstances in which cellular proteostasis is acutely strained: treatment with azetidine-2-carboxylic acid (AZC), a proline analog that interferes with nascent protein folding, resulting in aggregation (Trotter et al., 2002), or overexpression of an aggregation-prone mutant protein (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Trotter et al., 2002 and Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011.

claim: Cells activate Hsf1 within minutes after rRNA processing is disrupted.
source: Comparison of the kinetics of pre-rRNA and Hsf1-dependent transcript accumulation revealed that cells activate Hsf1 within minutes after rRNA processing is disrupted, indicating a rapid strain on proteostasis, as observed in instantaneous heat shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing kinetics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: During the first 15–30 min of low-dose rapamycin treatment, cells strongly repress synthesis of r-proteins while maintaining normal levels of rRNA transcription.
source: During the first 15–30 min of low-dose rapamycin treatment, cells strongly repress synthesis of r-proteins while maintaining normal levels of rRNA transcription (Reiter et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reiter et al., 2011.

claim: Precursor rRNA accumulated during rapamycin treatment due to r-protein limitation.
source: Precursor rRNA accumulated due to r-protein limitation, as expected, but the Hsf1-dependent gene BTN2 was not upregulated during rapamycin treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The Hsf1-dependent gene BTN2 was not upregulated during rapamycin treatment.
source: Precursor rRNA accumulated due to r-protein limitation, as expected, but the Hsf1-dependent gene BTN2 was not upregulated during rapamycin treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Halting translation with cycloheximide (CHX) resulted in pre-rRNA accumulation but no upregulation of BTN2.
source: Similarly, halting translation, and thus r-protein synthesis, with cycloheximide (CHX) resulted in pre-rRNA accumulation but no upregulation of BTN2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, though the specific figure reference is in Figure 1G based on context.

claim: When r-proteins are in excess relative to what can be assembled into ribosomes, yielding orphan r-proteins, cells activate a proteostatic stress response driven by Hsf1.
source: On the basis of these findings, we conclude that when r-proteins are in excess relative to what can be assembled into ribosomes, yielding orphan r-proteins, cells activate a proteostatic stress response driven by Hsf1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing differential Hsf1 activation depending on whether r-proteins or rRNA are in excess.

claim: Diazaborine (DZA) blocks cytoplasmic assembly of several r-proteins into the 60S subunit by specifically inhibiting the ATPase Drg1.
source: To this end, we treated cells with a small molecule, diazaborine (DZA), that blocks cytoplasmic assembly of several r-proteins into the 60S subunit by specifically inhibiting the ATPase Drg1 (Loibl et al., 2014) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loibl et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Screens for DZA resistance have yielded only mutations in factors involved in drug efflux and the gene encoding the drug's mechanistic target, DRG1, indicating that the compound is highly specific.
source: Screens for DZA resistance have yielded only mutations in factors involved in drug efflux and the gene encoding the drug's mechanistic target, DRG1, indicating that the compound is highly specific (Wendler et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wendler et al., 1997.

claim: Over a time-course of moderate, sublethal DZA treatment, the Hsf1-dependent transcripts BTN2 and HSP82 strongly accumulated by 15 min.
source: Over a time-course of moderate, sublethal DZA treatment, the Hsf1-dependent transcripts BTN2 and HSP82 strongly accumulated by 15 min, whereas the Msn2/4-dependent transcript HSP12 exhibited no response (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Msn2/4-dependent transcript HSP12 exhibited no response to DZA treatment.
source: Over a time-course of moderate, sublethal DZA treatment, the Hsf1-dependent transcripts BTN2 and HSP82 strongly accumulated by 15 min, whereas the Msn2/4-dependent transcript HSP12 exhibited no response (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hsf1-dependent transcripts returned to basal levels at 90 min after DZA treatment, indicating that Hsf1 activation was an adaptive response.
source: Moreover, Hsf1-dependent transcripts returned to basal levels at 90 min, indicating that Hsf1 activation was an adaptive response.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the kinetic data showing transient Hsf1 activation.

claim: A DZA-resistant point mutant of Drg1 (V725E) restored cell growth and reduced accumulation of Hsf1-dependent transcripts.
source: Importantly, a DZA-resistant point mutant of Drg1 (V725E) (Loibl et al., 2014) restored cell growth and reduced accumulation of Hsf1-dependent transcripts, confirming that DZA contributes to Hsf1 activation via the expected mechanism (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Loibl et al., 2014.

claim: DZA treatment protected cells from subsequent lethal heat stress (thermotolerance).
source: Consistent with a functional role of Hsf1 activation, we found that DZA treatment protected cells from subsequent lethal heat stress (thermotolerance) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cells treated with DZA for 15 or 45 min, RNA-seq revealed activation of Hsf1-dependent proteostasis genes in the absence of Msn2/4-dependent general stress genes.
source: In cells treated with DZA for 15 or 45 min, RNA-seq revealed activation of the same response that was induced by depletion of rRNA processing factors: upregulation of Hsf1-dependent proteostasis genes in the absence of Msn2/4-dependent general stress genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By 45 min of DZA treatment, cells upregulated proteasome subunits ~ 2 fold.
source: Furthermore, by 45 min, cells upregulated proteasome subunits ~ 2 fold, consistent with the early Hsf1-dependent upregulation of the proteasome-regulatory transcription factor RPN4 (Figure 2D) (Fleming et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Fleming et al., 2002.

claim: The canonical unfolded protein response (UPR), which responds to misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, was not activated by either DZA or depletion of rRNA processing factors.
source: Consistent with the exceptional specificity of this perturbation in eliciting an Hsf1-dependent response, we found that the canonical unfolded protein response (UPR), which responds to misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, was not activated by either DZA or depletion of rRNA processing factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Depletion of the Rps26 escortin Tsr2 led to accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA.
source: Each escortin was depleted ~70% by 20 min. Northern blots revealed accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Depletion of the Sqt1 (Rpl10) escortin led to accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA.
source: Each escortin was depleted ~70% by 20 min. Northern blots revealed accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Depletion of the Yar1 (Rps3) escortin led to accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA.
source: Each escortin was depleted ~70% by 20 min. Northern blots revealed accumulation of BTN2 and HSP82 mRNAs by 10–20 min, with no change in the level of Msn2/4-regulated HSP12 mRNA (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Either by inhibition of Drg1 or depletion of escortins, orphan r-proteins are sufficient to activate the Hsf1 regulon.
source: Thus, either by inhibition of Drg1 or depletion of escortins, orphan r-proteins are sufficient to activate the Hsf1 regulon.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing Hsf1 activation in both conditions.

claim: The set of downregulated genes in RPAS comprised mostly r-protein genes.
source: Intriguingly, the set of downregulated genes comprised mostly r-protein genes (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Under many stress conditions, both r-protein genes and assembly factor genes, collectively termed the ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) regulon, are repressed through Tor-dependent signaling.
source: Under many stress conditions, both r-protein genes and assembly factor genes, collectively termed the ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) regulon, are repressed through Tor-dependent signaling (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Marion et al., 2004; Urban et al., 2007) (e.g. oxidative stress by diamide, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jorgensen et al., 2004; Marion et al., 2004; Urban et al., 2007 and data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Cells treated with DZA for 15 or 45 min exhibited no change in the level of the TORC1 activity reporter, phosphorylated (phos-) Rps6.
source: Indeed, cells treated with DZA for 15 or 45 min exhibited no change in the level of the TORC1 activity reporter, phosphorylated (phos-) Rps6 (González et al., 2015) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F and citation to González et al., 2015.

claim: All ORFs tested, including GFP-V5, accumulated to lower levels when cells were treated with DZA, consistent with a rapid reduction in translational output under RPAS.
source: All ORFs, including GFP-V5, accumulated to lower levels when cells were treated with DZA, consistent with a rapid reduction in translational output under RPAS (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DZA treatment achieved a >50% reduction in protein synthesis, which cannot be explained by a diminishing ribosome pool (maximal reduction of 20% in 20 min).
source: Because DZA could achieve a maximal reduction of 20% in the ribosome pool in a 20-min experiment, this >50% reduction in synthesis cannot be explained by a diminishing ribosome pool.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing the observed reduction in synthesis to the theoretical maximum from ribosome dilution.

claim: The reduction in translational capacity during RPAS is not mediated through the kinase Gcn2, as phosphorylated (phos-) eIF2α did not accumulate during DZA treatment.
source: Interestingly, the reduction in translational capacity is not mediated through the kinase Gcn2 as in other stresses such as carbon or nitrogen starvation and oxidative stress, as phosphorylated (phos-) eIF2α did not accumulate during DZA treatment (Cherkasova and Hinnebusch, 2003; Dever et al., 1992; Shenton et al., 2006) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F and citations to Cherkasova and Hinnebusch, 2003; Dever et al., 1992; Shenton et al., 2006.

claim: Several r-proteins are found to aggregate in the absence of general cotranslational folding machinery, post-translational escortins, or nuclear import machinery.
source: Several r-proteins are found to aggregate in the absence of general cotranslational folding machinery, post-translational escortins, or nuclear import machinery (Jäkel et al., 2002; Koplin et al., 2010; Pillet et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jäkel et al., 2002; Koplin et al., 2010; Pillet et al., 2017.

claim: Excess r-proteins are targeted for degradation by Excess Ribosomal Protein Quality Control (ERISQ), a ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated pathway.
source: Further, excess r-proteins are targeted for degradation by Excess Ribosomal Protein Quality Control (ERISQ), a ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated pathway, in the absence of which r-proteins likewise prevalently aggregate (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a and Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: Hsf1 activation by DZA required ongoing translation: pre-treatment with CHX prevented upregulation of Hsf1 targets.
source: Supporting this idea, we found that Hsf1 activation by DZA required ongoing translation: pre-treatment with CHX prevented upregulation of Hsf1 targets, supporting the model of proteotoxic orphan r-proteins (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hsf1 activation by depletion of the rRNA processing factor Rat1 was fully inhibited by CHX pre-treatment.
source: Similarly, Hsf1 activation by depletion of the rRNA processing factor Rat1 was fully inhibited by CHX pre-treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RPAS induced by DZA treatment resulted in no gross protein aggregation, even at 40 min.
source: By contrast, RPAS induced by DZA treatment resulted in no such gross protein aggregation, even at 40 min.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to AZC treatment in the protein aggregation assay, as shown in the context of Figure 4C.

claim: Newly synthesized Rps26, Rpl10, and Rpl3 shifted three- to fivefold to the insoluble fraction upon DZA treatment.
source: We found that newly synthesized Rps26, Rpl10, and Rpl3 shifted three- to fivefold to the insoluble fraction upon DZA treatment (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D,F.

claim: The levels of Rpl4 and Rps3 in the pellet increased modestly if at all upon DZA treatment.
source: Interestingly, the levels of Rpl4 and Rps3 in the pellet increased modestly if at all, possibly due to their distinct biochemical characteristics, protection from aggregation by chaperones, or rapid assembly into precursor ribosome subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Treating extracts with the nuclease benzonase did not solubilize aggregated r-proteins, indicating that they were not in RNA- or DNA-dependent assemblies.
source: Treating extracts with the nuclease benzonase did not solubilize aggregated r-proteins, indicating that they were not in RNA- or DNA-dependent assemblies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After DZA treatment, only a modest amount of mature, assembled r-proteins (Rpl10 and Rpl3) were present in the pellet, likely due to the small unassembled fraction.
source: After DZA treatment, only a modest amount of tagged r-proteins were present in the pellet, likely due to the small unassembled fraction (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E,F with inference about the mechanism.

claim: A broad complement of r-proteins accumulate in aggregates following DZA treatment.
source: We performed quantitative mass spectrometry to test the generality of r-protein aggregation during RPAS, and found that a broad complement of r-proteins accumulate in aggregates following DZA treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A clear and general shift of r-proteins to the aggregate fraction was observed following DZA treatment, beyond those that are directly downstream of Drg1 function in the cytosol.
source: Nevertheless, we observed a clear and general shift of r-proteins to the aggregate fraction following DZA treatment, beyond those that are directly downstream of Drg1 (the target of DZA) function in the cytosol (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: A prominent group of nucleolar ribosome biogenesis factors were found amongst the strongest aggregators in DZA.
source: In addition to finding r-proteins, particularly those that are in the large 60S subunit, amongst the strongest aggregators in DZA, we found a prominent group of nucleolar ribosome biogenesis factors (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: DZA treatment leads to aggregation of r-proteins assembled in the nucleus and collateral aggregation of nucleolar ribosome biogenesis factors.
source: These data suggest that, in addition to causing aggregation of r-proteins downstream of Drg1 function in the cytosol, DZA treatment leads to aggregation of r-proteins assembled in the nucleus and collateral aggregation of nucleolar ribosome biogenesis factors (Figure 4F,G,H).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mass spectrometry data showing aggregation of nuclear r-proteins and biogenesis factors.

claim: Upon treatment with DZA, Sis1 drastically relocalized within the nucleus, moving to the nuclear periphery, where it formed a ring-like structure.
source: Upon treatment with DZA, Sis1 drastically relocalized within the nucleus, moving to the nuclear periphery, where it formed a ring-like structure (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Upon DZA treatment, Cfi1 relocalized from the periphery toward the middle of the nucleus, adjacent to the Sis1 ring structure.
source: At the same time, Cfi1 relocalized from the periphery toward the middle of the nucleus, adjacent to the Sis1 ring structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in the context of Figure 5A–C.

claim: The effect of DZA on Sis1 and Cfi1 was completely blocked by inhibiting translation with CHX.
source: The effect of DZA on Sis1 and Cfi1 was completely blocked by inhibiting translation with CHX, consistent with the idea that newly synthesized orphan r-proteins drove the response.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data with inference about the mechanism.

claim: Treatment with DZA increased the number of cytosolic Hsp104 foci, to seven or eight per cell, likely reflecting CytoQ body formation in response to orphan r-proteins.
source: Treatment with DZA increased the number of cytosolic Hsp104 foci, to seven or eight per cell, likely reflecting CytoQ body formation in response to orphan r-proteins (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D with inference about the mechanism.

claim: The orphan r-proteins produced as a result of DZA treatment disrupt proteostasis in the cytosol and the nucleus.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that the orphan r-proteins produced as a result of DZA treatment disrupt proteostasis in the cytosol and the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the microscopy data showing relocalization of proteostasis factors in both compartments.

claim: hsf1 po4* cells grew at wild-type rates at 30°C but were very sick under proteotoxic conditions (AZC or 37°C).
source: We found that hsf1 po4* cells grew at wild-type rates at 30°C but were very sick under proteotoxic conditions (AZC or 37°C), demonstrating that the hsf1 po4* allele lacks the ability to cope with proteotoxic stress (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: hsf1 po4* cells were nearly incapable of growth in DZA.
source: hsf1 po4* were nearly incapable of growth in DZA (Figure 6B), highlighting the critical role of wild-type Hsf1 in the adaptation to RPAS.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of the transcription factor RPN4 conferred a substantial growth defect in the presence of DZA (~25 fold more severe than in the absence of drug on day 3).
source: However, loss of the transcription factor RPN4, which controls the basal and stress-induced levels of the proteasome (Fleming et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2008), conferred a substantial growth defect in the presence of DZA (~25 fold more severe than in the absence of drug on day 3), at 37°C, and in the presence of AZC (Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 6D and citations to Fleming et al., 2002 and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Loss of the only non-essential proteasome subunit, PRE9, made cells DZA-resistant.
source: We also found that loss of the only non-essential proteasome subunit, PRE9, made cells DZA-resistant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pretreatment with estradiol to activate Hsf1DBD-VP16 yielded a > 40% growth enhancement in DZA that was independent of changes to cell size.
source: Pretreatment with estradiol yielded a > 40% growth enhancement in DZA that was independent of changes to cell size. Similar effects were observed after growth in AZC, which induces global proteotoxicity, whereas only a 9% growth rate increase was observed for vehicle-treated cells (Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: When challenged with DZA, cells grown in glycerol demonstrated a lower level of Hsf1 target gene activation compared to cells grown in glucose.
source: When challenged with DZA, cells grown in glycerol demonstrated a lower level of Hsf1 target gene activation (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: sch9Δ cells showed lower levels of Hsf1 target gene activation by DZA compared to wild-type cells.
source: As with wild-type cells in glycerol, sch9Δ cells showed lower levels of Hsf1 target gene activation by DZA (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: DZA treatment altered the processing of rRNA under all conditions tested.
source: Importantly, we observed that DZA treatment altered the processing of rRNA under all conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), validating that ribosome assembly was being disrupted.
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proteotoxic strain was stronger in cells with higher rates of ribosome production.
source: Thus, the proteotoxic strain was stronger in cells with higher rates of ribosome production, indicating that proliferating cells are at a stronger risk of experiencing RPAS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing Hsf1 activation in cells with different growth rates.

claim: Proliferating cells are at a stronger risk of experiencing RPAS.
source: Thus, the proteotoxic strain was stronger in cells with higher rates of ribosome production, indicating that proliferating cells are at a stronger risk of experiencing RPAS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Excess orphan r-proteins that arise from aberrations in ribosome biogenesis drive proteotoxicity and impact cellular fitness under r-protein assembly stress.
source: Here, we report an extraribosomal consequence of aberrant ribosome assembly: collapse of proteostasis resolved by an Hsf1-dependent response. We propose a model wherein excess orphan r-proteins that arise from aberrations in ribosome biogenesis drive proteotoxicity and impact cellular fitness under r-protein assembly stress (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The master proteostasis transcription factor Hsf1 is activated to increase the abundance of folding and degradation machineries, likely following sequestration of chaperones such as Hsp40 and Hsp70 by r-protein aggregates.
source: In turn, the master proteostasis transcription factor Hsf1 is activated to increase the abundance of folding and degradation machineries, likely following sequestration of chaperones such as Hsp40 and Hsp70 by r-protein aggregates (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim combines experimental observations with inference about the mechanism, supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2016.

claim: The proteostatic response supports cell fitness and is capable of protecting cells from r-protein assembly stress.
source: The proteostatic response supports cell fitness and is capable of protecting cells from r-protein assembly stress.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results showing improved fitness with Hsf1 activation.

claim: Several r-proteins are produced in excess in human tissue culture cells and are rapidly targeted for degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Interestingly, several r-proteins are produced in excess, for instance in human tissue culture cells, and are rapidly targeted for degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Abovich et al., 1985; Lam et al., 2007; McShane et al., 2016; Sung et al., 2016a, Sung et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abovich et al., 1985; Lam et al., 2007; McShane et al., 2016; Sung et al., 2016a, Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: In the perturbations modeled in this work, cells are challenged with a larger proportion of orphan r-proteins that overwhelms the canonical clearance mechanisms, necessitating an increase in proteostasis capacity.
source: We therefore propose that in the perturbations modeled in this work, cells are challenged with a larger proportion of orphan r-proteins that overwhelms the canonical clearance mechanisms, necessitating an increase in proteostasis capacity, consistent with the importance of both Hsf1 and Rpn4 in RPAS (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: DNA-damaging chemotherapeutic agents like etoposide, camptothecin, and 5-fluorouracil and transcription inhibitors like actinomycin D disrupt the nucleolus and rRNA processing.
source: For example, DNA-damaging chemotherapeutic agents like etoposide, camptothecin, and 5-fluorouracil and transcription inhibitors like actinomycin D disrupt the nucleolus and rRNA processing (Burger et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burger et al., 2010.

claim: Several Hsf1 targets are upregulated by and may be important in responding to DNA damaging agents.
source: Indeed, several Hsf1 targets are seen upregulated by and may be important in responding to DNA damaging agents (Miller et al., 2015a; Tkach et al., 2012; Workman et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2015a; Tkach et al., 2012; Workman et al., 2006.

claim: Environmental stressors such as heat shock deform the nucleolus.
source: Environmental stressors such as heat shock also deform the nucleolus, and many other stressors in yeast cause accumulation of pre-rRNA (Boulon et al., 2010; Kos-Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boulon et al., 2010 and Kos-Braun et al., 2017.

claim: Many stressors in yeast cause accumulation of pre-rRNA.
source: Environmental stressors such as heat shock also deform the nucleolus, and many other stressors in yeast cause accumulation of pre-rRNA (Boulon et al., 2010; Kos-Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boulon et al., 2010 and Kos-Braun et al., 2017.

claim: Imbalanced production of r-proteins arises in mutations found in ribosomopathies, as well as in aging and cancer.
source: Imbalanced production of r-proteins arises in mutations found in ribosomopathies, as well as in aging (David et al., 2010) and cancer (Guimaraes and Zavolan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to David et al., 2010 and Guimaraes and Zavolan, 2016.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis fluctuates in response to nutrient availability, stress, cell growth, and differentiation cues.
source: Because ribosome biogenesis is not a constitutive process, but instead fluctuates in response to nutrient availability, stress, cell growth, and differentiation cues (Lempiäinen and Shore, 2009; Mayer and Grummt, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lempiäinen and Shore, 2009 and Mayer and Grummt, 2006.

claim: The severity of the phenotype resulting from disrupted ribosome biogenesis may relate to cell growth rate and the required level of ribosome production in a cell type/state.
source: The severity of the resulting phenotype may relate to cell growth rate and the required level of ribosome production in a cell type/state (Figure 7A,B), which suggests a possible mechanism for why certain cell types are especially vulnerable to disrupted ribosome biogenesis, such as in ribosomopathies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Aggregates can sequester other proteins with essential functions.
source: While the molecular basis for how protein aggregates compromise cell health is not fully understood, one demonstrated possibility is that aggregates sequester other proteins with essential functions (Olzscha et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Olzscha et al., 2011.

claim: Alleviating proteotoxic stress enhances cell growth under RPAS.
source: Thus, the proteotoxic stress elicited by RPAS has the potential to severely disrupt cellular homeostasis, consistent with our findings that alleviating proteotoxic stress enhances cell growth under RPAS (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Yeast and human cells degrade r-proteins produced in excess, and cells lacking this quality control mechanism contain aggregated r-proteins.
source: Consistent with this, yeast and human cells degrade r-proteins produced in excess, and cells lacking this quality control mechanism contain aggregated r-proteins (McShane et al., 2016; Sung et al., 2016a, Sung et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McShane et al., 2016; Sung et al., 2016a, Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response is activated when assembly of mitochondrial complexes is disrupted.
source: Similarly, the mitochondrial unfolded protein response is activated when assembly of mitochondrial complexes is disrupted (Yoneda et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoneda et al., 2004.

claim: Blocking import of organellar proteins into the ER or mitochondria results in cytosolic proteotoxic stress.
source: Blocking import of organellar proteins into the ER or mitochondria results in cytosolic proteotoxic stress (Brandman et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Wrobel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brandman et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Wrobel et al., 2015.

claim: The nucleolus is morphologically disrupted and recruits chaperones such as Hsp70 under stress, including heat shock and proteasome inhibition.
source: Given that the nucleolus is morphologically disrupted and recruits chaperones such as Hsp70 under stress, including heat shock and proteasome inhibition (Lam et al., 2007; Liu et al., 1996; Pelham, 1984)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lam et al., 2007; Liu et al., 1996; Pelham, 1984.

claim: New r-proteins undergo ubiquitination, localize in protein aggregates, and associate with chaperones under heat shock.
source: Consistently, new r-proteins undergo ubiquitination, localize in protein aggregates, and associate with chaperones under heat shock (Fang et al., 2014; Ruan et al., 2017; Shalgi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fang et al., 2014; Ruan et al., 2017; Shalgi et al., 2013.

claim: Erythroid differentiation is highly reliant on Hsp70 availability, as evidenced by the fact that Hsp70 sequestration can result in the anemic phenotype of beta-thalassemia.
source: Erythroid differentiation is highly reliant on Hsp70 availability, as evidenced by the fact that Hsp70 sequestration can result in the anemic phenotype of beta-thalassemia (Arlet et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arlet et al., 2014.

claim: Cancer cells are sensitized to small molecules that dampen the proteostasis network.
source: Similarly, cancer cells are sensitized to small molecules that dampen the proteostasis network (Balch et al., 2008; Joshi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balch et al., 2008 and Joshi et al., 2018.

claim: Exogenous activation of the Hsf1 regulon protects yeast from RPAS.
source: In this work, we showed that exogenous activation of the Hsf1 regulon protects yeast from RPAS.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results showing improved growth with estradiol-induced Hsf1 activation.
